items.text: من أنواع الـ. What's، uh، plural of طير؟

versions.name: nawa3 min anwaa3 el- + plural
versions.one_line: To say something is a kind of X, say 'a kind from the kinds of' (nawa3 min anwaa3 el-) followed by the plural of X, or say waa7ad min anwaa3 el-; it looks like a 'type of types' but it works.
versions.formula: nawa3 / waa7ad + min + anwaa3 + el- + plural noun

examples.english: What kinds of doctors are there?
What kinds of dairy are there?

versions.why: She said the student could say 'one of the types of birds' or 'a type of types', which does not make sense in English, and then asked for the plural of طير to finish it.

checked.why: P-b35e2602 teaches 'waa7ad min el-' + plural, but nobody covers 'nawa3 min anwaa3 el-' + plural or 'anwaa3 el-' + plural meaning 'kinds of'.

items.text: It could be with any verb actually. يعني for example, أنا اشتغلت عنك.

versions.name: 3an = on someone's behalf
versions.one_line: Put 3an + the person after a verb to say you did or felt it in place of someone who should have done it.
versions.formula: verb + 3an + person (ending)
versions.why: She explained that 3an works with any verb when you do something that someone else should have done, which is not the same as working for an employer.

overlaps.name: verb + its fixed preposition
overlaps.why: It is a preposition chosen after a verb, but here 3an adds a meaning (on behalf of) and is not a fixed partner of one verb.

checked.why: No existing rule or proposal teaches 3an + person for doing or feeling something on someone's behalf; D1 and D2 only cover prepositions in general.

items.text: We wouldn't use آخر we would use ماضي.

versions.name: aa5er = last in order, maadi = past
versions.one_line: Use aa5er for last in a sequence (the final one); for last meaning the previous or past one (last summer), use maadi.
versions.formula: aa5er = last in sequence; noun + el-maadi = last (past) noun
versions.why: English uses 'last' for both the final one and the previous one, but she said aa5er only means last in a sequence, and maadi means past.

overlaps.name: aa5er / a5eer: before or after the noun
overlaps.why: A15 covers where aa5er goes around the noun, not when to use maadi instead.

checked.why: A15 covers aa5er as 'last' in sequence, but none of the rules or proposals teach using maadi (el-maadi) for 'last' meaning the past or previous one.

items.text: بس شركة because it's feminine, you would say تبعتي.

versions.name: tabe3 agrees with the noun
versions.one_line: To say 'my own' business, use tabe3 + the ending, and with a feminine noun it becomes tab3a: sharike tab3ti.
versions.formula: noun + tabe3 / tab3at + ending

examples.arabic: بس شركة because it's feminine, you would say تبعتي.
examples.english: for a feminine noun like company, use tab3ati (mine)

versions.why: She said you can use tabe3 for 'business', and that it changes to tab3at with a feminine noun.

overlaps.name: possessive endings
overlaps.why: It is also a way to say 'my', but it uses a separate word, tabe3, that agrees with the noun.

checked.why: No existing rule or proposal teaches tabe3 / tab3a as a possessive word that agrees with its noun; A4 only covers endings attached directly to the noun.

items.text: Time, occurrence, if it's occurrence or turn or it's, it's marra. You would say my last time, my first time, it's all marra if you make it in this context.

versions.name: time as occurrence = marra
versions.one_line: When 'time' means an occasion or a turn (my last time, my first time), say marra and not wa2t.
versions.formula: aa5er / awal + marra

examples.arabizi: haadi ra7 tkoon aa5er marra ili honaak
examples.arabic: haadi ra7 tkoon aa5er marra ili honaak
examples.english: This will be my last time there

versions.why: English uses one word, 'time', for an occasion and for a stretch of time, but she said an occasion or turn is marra.

checked.why: No existing rule or proposal covers using marra (not wa2t) for 'time' as an occasion or turn, as in aa5er marra / awal marra.

items.text: we give them the she verb conjugations, and we give them the feminine adjectives

versions.name: non-human plurals act feminine
versions.one_line: Plurals of non-human things (lessons, cars, houses) are not truly feminine, but they are treated as feminine singular: they get the she-form of the verb and the feminine singular adjective.
versions.formula: non-human plural + she-verb / feminine singular adjective
versions.why: She explained that about 90% of plurals are non-human and take the feminine singular treatment (adjectives, verbs, even prepositions like فيها). It does not apply to human plurals like أولاد, and English speakers expect a plural verb and adjective to match the plural noun.

overlaps.name: verb matches its subject
overlaps.why: B18 says the verb matches its subject, but here a plural noun takes the feminine singular form instead of a plural form.

checked.why: A8, A18 and B18 cover gender and agreement in general, but none says non-human plurals take the she-verb and the feminine singular adjective.

items.text: أول مرة إلي

versions.name: my first: awal + noun + ili
versions.one_line: To say 'my first / my last / my second', put the ordinal before the noun and add إلي (or إلها, etc.) after it, instead of putting a possessive ending on the noun (مرتي means 'my wife').
versions.formula: awal / aa5er / taani + noun + ili (ilha, ilhom...)
versions.why: English speakers add the possessive to the noun (marti), which Arabic hears as 'my wife'; Arabic uses ili after the noun. Amal said the other way, with the adjective after a possessive noun, is technically right but you would never hear it.

overlaps.name: mufaddal + 3ind
overlaps.why: A23 also covers 3ind with mufaddal, while this rule uses ili for other ordinals.

checked.why: No existing rule or proposal teaches putting إلي/إلها after an ordinal + noun to say 'my first/last'; A13, A15 and A20 only cover the plain meanings and the el-/possessive cases.

versions.name: my first: ordinal + noun + ili
versions.one_line: To say 'my first / my second / my third / my last', put the ordinal before the noun and add إلي (or إلها, إلو, etc.) after it, instead of putting a possessive ending on the noun (مرتي means 'my wife'). With an owner noun, use إل + the owner: آخر سيارة إلإمها.
versions.formula: ordinal (awal / taani / talet / raabe3 / aa5er...) + noun + ili (ilha, ilo...) or ordinal + noun + il + owner
versions.why: English speakers add the possessive to the noun (marti), which Arabic hears as 'my wife'; Arabic uses ili after the noun. Amal said the other way, with the adjective after a possessive noun, is technically right but you would never hear it.

overlaps.name: mufaddal + 3ind
overlaps.why: A23 also covers 3ind with mufaddal, while this rule uses ili for ordinals.

versions.asked: Good rule but can be applied to tani, aa5er and the other ordinals like third and forth etc. so make it more general not strictly for awal and add idafa words like her mom last car for example, or his send cup of of coffee.

items.text: فيو، in it.

versions.name: fi + ending for contains
versions.one_line: To say a thing has something inside it, like homework with three questions, use fi plus the ending (fiyo, 'in it'), not 3ind.
versions.formula: thing + fi + ending + number + noun

examples.english: It has three questions in it.

versions.why: She corrected the student's 3indo with fiyo, explaining that this is not 'has' but 'in it', which English speakers get wrong by translating 'has' as 3ind.

overlaps.name: endings on prepositions
overlaps.why: It also puts the person ending on a preposition (fi), but the point is choosing fi over 3ind for 'contains'.

checked.why: No existing rule or proposal teaches fi + ending (fiyo, 'in it') for saying a thing contains something; D3 only covers endings on prepositions in general, and 3ind is not contrasted.

versions.name: fi + ending for contains
versions.one_line: English says 'have' for anything that holds something, but in Arabic 3ind is not used for that: when a thing contains something, like homework with three questions or a street with cars, use fi plus the ending (fiyo, 'in it') instead.
versions.formula: thing + fi + ending + number + noun

examples.english: It has three questions in it.

versions.why: English speakers use 'have' for everything, but not every thing can 'have' in Arabic: a street can't have cars, it contains cars, so fi replaces 'have' and 3ind is the mistake.

overlaps.name: endings on prepositions
overlaps.why: It also puts the person ending on a preposition (fi), but the point is choosing fi over 3ind for 'contains'.

versions.asked:
Make it more clearer that sometimes fi replaces have in English.
Not everything can take have like English.
For example, a street can’t have cars, but it contains cars

items.text: لا، بيت is you getting moved. So كل إشي gets moved.

versions.name: bit- verb means gets done
versions.one_line: A verb starting with bit- means the subject gets acted on (gets moved), whereas the plain b- form means you do it to something.
versions.formula: bit- + verb = subject gets X-ed (كل إشي بيت حرك = everything gets moved)
versions.why: The student said بيحرك, which would mean 'moves something', but she explained that for 'everything is moving' you need بيت, the 'getting moved' form.

overlaps.name: make-X vs get-X
overlaps.why: B12 also contrasts a 'make someone do' form with a 'get/become' form of the verb.

checked.why: No existing rule or proposal covers the bit- (passive/gets done) verb form versus the active b- form; B12 is about doubling the middle letter, which is a different choice.

items.text: لا، لا، وحدة because she's feminine. وحدة. Cuz she's someone feminine.

versions.name: wa7de min + plural
versions.one_line: To say 'one of my friends', use wa7ad or wa7de followed by min and the plural noun. wa7de is for a girl or woman; the plural noun stays general.
versions.formula: wa7ad / wa7de + min + plural noun (+ my)

examples.english: it is one of the words

versions.why: She explained that wa7de is feminine because the friend is a woman, while s7aabi (friends) stays general and does not limit the group to women.

checked.why: No existing rule or proposal teaches 'one of (my) X' as wa7ad/wa7de + min + plural; the nearby P-FA-89701583 is about waa7ad after ordinals, which is a different choice.

versions.name: wa7ad / wa7de: when to use
versions.one_line: To say 'one of my friends', use wa7ad or wa7de followed by min and the plural noun; wa7de is for a girl or woman, and the plural noun stays general. After this / that / these, don't add wa7ad or wa7de (this bag is better than that one = haadi el-shanta a7san min hadeek), and for 'the better ones', '
versions.formula: wa7ad / wa7de + min + plural noun (+ my); but no wa7ad / wa7de after this / that / these or for 'the red ones'

This bag is better than that one

items.text: إذا لازم، إذا لازم أختار. There's no all of these should, could, would. We don't have them.

versions.name: no should/could: laazem, mumkin
versions.one_line: Arabic has no separate should, could or would. Say 'if I have to choose' with iza laazem, and use mumkin for 'could'.
versions.formula: iza laazem + verb / mumkin + verb
versions.why: English speakers reach for should, could and would, but she said Arabic does not have them and uses laazem or mumkin instead.

overlaps.name: b-drop after modals
overlaps.why: B2 covers dropping the b- after want, must and can words, but not using laazem or mumkin in place of should, could and would.

checked.why: B16 covers kaan laazem and B2 covers verbs after modals, but none says Arabic has no should/could/would, or teaches iza laazem for 'if I have to' and mumkin for 'could'.

items.text: we say 300 because مية is feminine so 300 شخص

versions.name: feminine number before miyye
versions.one_line: For hundreds, use the feminine form of the number (ثلاث مية) because مية is feminine, and the counted noun after it is singular.
versions.formula: feminine number + مية + singular noun

examples.arabic: we say 300 because مية is feminine so 300 شخص
examples.english: we say 300 because مية is feminine, so 300 شخص (300 people)

versions.why: She explained that مية is feminine, so the number in front of it takes the feminine form, and that 300 is more than 10, so the noun after it is singular.

overlaps.name: number + noun
overlaps.why: E1 covers singular after 11+, but not the feminine number form in front of مية.

checked.why: E1 only says 11+ takes a singular noun; it does not teach using the feminine number form before مية.

versions.name: hundreds add -t before noun
versions.one_line: Miyya is feminine, so it adds a -t when a noun comes after it; the number in front of it stays as it is (talatmiyya stays talatmiyya), and the noun after it is singular.
versions.formula: number + miyya (+ -t) + singular noun

examples.arabic: we say 300 because مية is feminine so 300 شخص
examples.english: we say 300 because مية is feminine, so 300 شخص (300 people)

versions.why: Miyya is a feminine word, so it takes the feminine -t when a noun follows; the number before it does not change.

overlaps.name: number + noun
overlaps.why: E1 covers the singular noun after 11+, and this hundreds rule belongs with it as an added note about the -t on miyya.

items.text:
using mufaddal. 
mufaddal (favorite) in Arabic varries. 
we treat it as an adjective that follows its noun with definiteness and gender. 
and because pronoun-ending nouns are considered definitive, we follow such nouns with el + mufaddal/e/a 
akli el-mufaddal = my favorite food.
makano el-mufaddal = his favorite place.
awaa3iha el-mufaddaleen = her favorite clothes. 

mufaddal + 3ind. 
sometimes, when favorite is put alone in a sentence with no noun, or the noun proceeds it, we use 3ind to support it. 

this is my favorite = had/i el-mufaddal 3indi 

we can also use 3ind anytime, not necessarily to support mufaddal when it's alone. 
hadi el-buza el-mufaddala 3indo = this is his favorite ice cream 
so t becomes a preference thing.

versions.name: mufaddal + 3ind
versions.one_line: Mufaddal (favorite) is an adjective that follows its noun and matches it in gender and definiteness; a noun with a pronoun ending counts as definite, so it takes el-mufaddal, and 3ind + the person can support it when it stands alone or after the noun.
versions.formula: noun-ending + el-mufaddal/e/a/een; el-mufaddal + 3ind + person

examples.english: this is his favorite ice cream

versions.why: English puts 'favorite' before the noun and never changes it, but in Arabic mufaddal comes after the noun and has to agree with it, and 3ind makes it a matter of preference.

overlaps.name: noun + adjective
overlaps.why: Mufaddal is an adjective that goes after its noun, and el- placement and gender follow the same noun + adjective pattern.

items.text:
a8lab + nafs
both a8lab nafs take a el + noun to mean most and same. 
nafs = same. 
nafs + el + noun = the same...
nafs el-tari2 = the same road. 
possessive/pronoun-ending nouns are also definitive. so nafs shanteti = same as my bag 

to say the same, we say nafs el-ishi. 

a8lab = most/ most of 
a8lab + el + noun = most / most of... 
 
a8lab el-naas = most people 
a8lab akli = most of my food. 
a8lab awaa3i sitti = most of my grandmother's clothes.

nafs loan juzdani = the same color as my purse/wallet

versions.name: a8lab and nafs + definite noun
versions.one_line: a8lab (most of) and nafs (the same) are followed by a definite noun, meaning el- + noun or a noun with a possessive ending.
versions.formula: a8lab / nafs + el- + noun (or noun + possessive ending)
versions.why: English says 'most people' and 'the same road' with no marker on the noun, but here the noun after a8lab or nafs must be definite, and a noun with a possessive ending already counts as definite.

overlaps.name: nafs + el-: the same
overlaps.why: A17 also covers nafs + el- + noun = the same, so a learner could mix up the two cards, while a8lab follows the same pattern with a different meaning.

items.text:
taani and 8eir 
Taani has two particularly useful functions: identifying something as second in a sequence and referring to something additional or different.
Rule 1: Taani + noun = Second / the second…
When taani comes before a noun, it can identify the second item or stage in a sequence.
Structure: taani + noun
Meaning: Second / the second…
Rule 2: El- + noun + el-taani / el-taaniye = The second / the other…
When el-taani or el-taaniye comes after the noun, it identifies a particular item as second or distinguishes it from another item.
Structure: el- + noun + el-taani / el-taaniye
Meaning: The second… / the other…
Rule 3: Noun + taani / taaniye = Another / a different…
When taani follows the noun without el-, it can mean another or a different one, rather than specifically the second item in a sequence.
Structure: noun + taani / taaniye
Meaning: Another… / a different…
Remember: The difference between second and another often depends on word order and context.
 
4. 8eir (غير): Different / Other
8eir is used to express difference or alternatives. Its interpretation depends on the phrase and context.
Rule 1: 8eir + noun = A different… / other…
When 8eir comes before a noun, it can introduce something different or other than what was previously mentioned.
Structure: 8eir + noun
Meaning: A different… / other…
8eir / mu5talef also takes the preposition (3an) when we want to say other than / different from. 
8eir can be used as an adjective as well and be put after the noun with "el" but it's rarely used and it's preferable to use it a function word. 
mu5talef is also different, but it's different from 8eir
• M5talef (مختلف) = different in nature or characteristics.
• 8eir (غير) = other than / another / something else.
They can overlap in meaning, but they are not interchangeable in every sentence.
items.example: taani 7ada = second person / the second person yoami el-tani = my second day, 8eir bluze = another/different shirt, ishi taani = something else, huwwe 8eir 3anni = he is different than me.

versions.name: taani and 8eir
versions.one_line: taani before a noun means second; after the noun without el- it means another; 8eir before a noun means a different or other one, and 8eir + 3an means different from.
versions.formula: taani + noun = second | el- + noun + el-taani = the second / the other | noun + taani = another | 8eir + noun = different / other
versions.why: English uses different words for second, another and different, but Arabic uses the same words, so the meaning depends on word order and context.

overlaps.name: taani: before or after the noun
overlaps.why: A14 also covers taani before or after the noun, with and without el-.

items.text:
Awal and aa5er uses 
in spoken Arabic, function words mean different things depending on where they're put in a sentence, whether they're followed by an "el" or not, or if an overruling grammar is present in the sentence. 
Awal can mean First / the first or the beginning of 
Awal + noun (without el) is first or the first. 
Awal + el + noun = the beginning of... 
a pronoun/possessive-ending noun is also considered a definitive noun: so awal yoami = the beginning of my day. 
to work around this rule, and because idafa always surpasses/overrules other grammar rules, we use ili or the adjective form of awal: awal (M) and oola (f) 
so my first day = yoami el-awal / awal yoam ili. 
to say first yyou can also use the adjective form. el-sayyara el-oola = the first car. 


aa5er is just like awal. 
aa5er yoam = last day, aa5er el-yoam = the end of the day, aa5er yoam ili / yoami el-a5eer = my last day, el-yoam el-a5eer = the last day.

versions.name: awal / aa5er with el-
versions.one_line: Awal and aa5er + a noun without el- mean first / last, but with el- or a possessive ending they mean the beginning / end of, so for 'my first day' use illi or put the adjective after the noun.
versions.formula: awal / aa5er + noun = first / last; awal / aa5er + el- or ending + noun = beginning / end of
versions.why: English uses 'first' and 'last' the same way everywhere, but in Arabic el- or a possessive ending on the noun turns them into 'the beginning of' and 'the end of', because idafa overrules the other rules.

overlaps.name: awal / oola: before or after the noun
overlaps.why: A13 already covers awal + noun versus awal + el- + noun, and a learner could mix it up with this rule.

versions.name: awal / aa5er with el-
versions.one_line: Awal and aa5er + a noun without el- mean first / last, but with el- or a possessive ending they mean the beginning / end of, so to say 'first' or 'last' there, use illi or put the adjective after the noun (el-awal / el-oola, el-a5eer).
versions.formula: awal / aa5er + noun = first / last; awal / aa5er + el- or ending + noun = beginning / end of; noun + el-awal / el-oola / el-a5eer or awal / aa5er + noun + ili = first / last
versions.why: English uses 'first' and 'last' the same way everywhere, but in Arabic el- or a possessive ending on the noun turns them into 'the beginning of' and 'the end of', because idafa overrules the other rules.

overlaps.name: awal / oola: before or after the noun
overlaps.why: A13 already covers awal + noun versus awal + el- + noun, and a learner could mix it up with this rule.

versions.asked: You can then updat the already there rule to include all awal and aa5er rules

items.text: كمان at the end. Don't worry about كمان.

versions.name: kamaan at the end = also
versions.one_line: To say 'also / too', put kamaan at the very end of the sentence, after the thing it adds to.
versions.formula: sentence + kamaan

examples.english: This is my fiancée's favorite dish too.

examples.arabic: هذي الأكلة المفضلة عند خطيبتي كمان.
examples.english: This dish is my fiancée's favorite too.

versions.why: English puts 'also' near the verb; she moved kamaan to the end of the sentence for 'too'.

versions.name: kamaan: also vs another
versions.one_line: Kamaan meaning 'also / too / as well' can go anywhere in the sentence, but kamaan meaning 'another / one more' goes before the noun.
versions.formula: also: kamaan anywhere | another: kamaan + noun

examples.arabizi: Heyye kamaan bet7eb el-baid / heyye bet7eb el-baid / kamaan heyye bet7eb el-baid

examples.english: This is my fiancée's favorite dish too.

examples.arabic: هذي الأكلة المفضلة عند خطيبتي كمان.
examples.english: This dish is my fiancée's favorite too.

versions.why: English uses two different words, 'also' and 'another', while Arabic uses kamaan for both, so only its place in the sentence shows which one is meant.
versions.asked:
For kamaan  to mean also, as well, or too,it doesn’t matter where it’s put in the sentence. 
It matters however, if  we want it to mean, one more or another (meaning more of the same thing)
To mean kamaan  as another of the same thing we put it before the knoun
Kamaan ishi = another / one more thing 
Heyye kamaan bet7eb el-baid / heyye bet7eb el-baid / kamaan heyye bet7eb el-baid = she also likes eggs

versions.name: hidden gender: nature words
versions.one_line: Some nature nouns look or sound masculine but are feminine (sun, fire, earth, sky), while هواء (air) is masculine even though it sounds feminine.
versions.formula: shams / nar / ard / sama = feminine; hawa = masculine

examples.english: So when does the sun rise?

versions.why: The gender of these nature nouns does not match their sound, so a learner cannot guess it from the word's shape.

overlaps.name: gender on adjectives

versions.name: hidden gender nouns
versions.one_line: Some nouns have a gender that does not match how they sound: they sound masculine but are feminine, or sound feminine but are masculine. This is not only for nature words (sun, fire, earth, sky, air) but also for words like hand, leg, eye, ear, girl and man.

examples.english: So when does the sun rise?

versions.why: The gender of these nouns does not match their sound, so a learner cannot guess it from the word's shape and has to learn each one.

payload.text:
Awal and aa5er uses 
in spoken Arabic, function words mean different things depending on where they're put in a sentence, whether they're followed by an "el" or not, or if an overruling grammar is present in the sentence. 
Awal can mean First / the first or the beginning of 
Awal + noun (without el) is first or the first. 
Awal + el + noun = the beginning of... 
a pronoun/possessive-ending noun is also considered a definitive noun: so awal yoami = the beginning of my day. 
to work around this rule, and because idafa always surpasses/overrules other grammar rules, we use ili or the adjective form of awal: awal (M) and oola (f) 
so my first day = yoami el-awal / awal yoam ili. 
to say first yyou can also use the adjective form. el-sayyara el-oola = the first car. 


aa5er is just like awal. 
aa5er yoam = last day, aa5er el-yoam = the end of the day, aa5er yoam ili / yoami el-a5eer = my last day, el-yoam el-a5eer = the last day.

taani and 8eir 
Taani has two particularly useful functions: identifying something as second in a sequence and referring to something additional or different.
Rule 1: Taani + noun = Second / the second…
When taani comes before a noun, it can identify the second item or stage in a sequence.
Structure: taani + noun
Meaning: Second / the second…
Rule 2: El- + noun + el-taani / el-taaniye = The second / the other…
When el-taani or el-taaniye comes after the noun, it identifies a particular item as second or distinguishes it from another item.
Structure: el- + noun + el-taani / el-taaniye
Meaning: The second… / the other…
Rule 3: Noun + taani / taaniye = Another / a different…
When taani follows the noun without el-, it can mean another or a different one, rather than specifically the second item in a sequence.
Structure: noun + taani / taaniye
Meaning: Another… / a different…
Remember: The difference between second and another often depends on word order and context.
 
4. 8eir (غير): Different / Other
8eir is used to express difference or alternatives. Its interpretation depends on the phrase and context.
Rule 1: 8eir + noun = A different… / other…
When 8eir comes before a noun, it can introduce something different or other than what was previously mentioned.
Structure: 8eir + noun
Meaning: A different… / other…
8eir / mu5talef also takes the preposition (3an) when we want to say other than / different from. 
8eir can be used as an adjective as well and be put after the noun with "el" but it's rarely used and it's preferable to use it a function word. 
mu5talef is also different, but it's different from 8eir
• M5talef (مختلف) = different in nature or characteristics.
• 8eir (غير) = other than / another / something else.
They can overlap in meaning, but they are not interchangeable in every sentence.
payload.example: taani 7ada = second person / the second person yoami el-tani = my second day, 8eir bluze = another/different shirt, ishi taani = something else, huwwe 8eir 3anni = he is different than me.

payload.text:
a8lab + nafs
both a8lab nafs take a el + noun to mean most and same. 
nafs = same. 
nafs + el + noun = the same...
nafs el-tari2 = the same road. 
possessive/pronoun-ending nouns are also definitive. so nafs shanteti = same as my bag 

to say the same, we say nafs el-ishi. 

a8lab = most/ most of 
a8lab + el + noun = most / most of... 
 
a8lab el-naas = most people 
a8lab akli = most of my food. 
a8lab awaa3i sitti = most of my grandmother's clothes.

nafs loan juzdani = the same color as my purse/wallet

using mufaddal. 
mufaddal (favorite) in Arabic varries. 
we treat it as an adjective that follows its noun with definiteness and gender. 
and because pronoun-ending nouns are considered definitive, we follow such nouns with el + mufaddal/e/a 
akli el-mufaddal = my favorite food.
makano el-mufaddal = his favorite place.
awaa3iha el-mufaddaleen = her favorite clothes. 

mufaddal + 3ind. 
sometimes, when favorite is put alone in a sentence with no noun, or the noun proceeds it, we use 3ind to support it. 

this is my favorite = had/i el-mufaddal 3indi 

we can also use 3ind anytime, not necessarily to support mufaddal when it's alone. 
hadi el-buza el-mufaddala 3indo = this is his favorite ice cream
